title: Pipili appliqué

paragraphs.text: In Rahul Mukherjee’s display photograph, circles repeat inside larger circles, with bright borders around them. The eye can follow one shape through the arrangement. That is a useful place to begin looking, before asking how the cloth was assembled.
D’source’s documented lampshade starts with coloured cloth cut and joined into appliqué. A cardboard stencil marks repeated outlines; the matching pieces are cut in layers and bundled for later use.

The appliqués are machine-stitched onto cloth in plain and decorative patterns. Wooden or iron rings then give the shade its shape. This is one documented process, not a description of every Pipili workshop.

Andrew Moore’s photograph brings the sewing machine into view beside the textile. It does not identify the maker or connect this piece to the lampshade example. Seeing a tool is a starting point for asking which stages it serves.
When speaking with a maker, ask about one edge or repeated shape. If you plan to buy, ask for the maker’s name, materials and care instructions, rather than trying to infer them from a photograph.

notes.text: Prof. Bibhudutta Baral, Divyadarshan C. S. and Manasa K H, NID Bengaluru, “Traditional Applique Work — Making Process,” D’source. Lampshade sequence.

Rahul Mukherjee. Pipili appliqué photographed in 2022. The image records a display, not current stock or a named maker’s catalogue. CC BY-SA 4.0. Resized and converted to WebP. No generated elements; derivative retains the stated share-alike licence.

Andrew Moore. A Pipili craftsperson at a sewing machine, photographed in 2016. The source does not name the maker. CC BY-SA 2.0. Resized and converted to WebP. No generated elements; derivative retains the stated share-alike licence.
